author: Mashzidul Tanun Borshon
title: Sundarbans permits in 2026: what actually changed, in plain language
excerpt: The forest office tightened vessel inspection and vessel-age limits, and the paperwork chain now runs through Mongla rather than Khulna. Here is what a guest needs to know, and what we file.

body.p: Every Sundarban trip in Bangladesh runs on two approvals: the forest-department entry permit for the reserve, and the vessel clearance for the boat that carries you. Neither is a formality, and neither is the traveller’s job if you booked with an operator who is on the approved list - but you should be able to tell us which route and which ghat we filed, and we will show you the paperwork.

Vessel inspection intervals were shortened and hull age is now checked against the licence rather than the insurance. In practice this retires a chunk of older mining boats from the tourist trade, which is good for safety and has pushed charter prices up 12-18% on the three-night routes. The second change is procedural: filings that used to close at the Khulna counter are now completed through Mongla, which adds a working day. We file on Tuesday for weekend departures.

body.h: The rules that will not change, and should not

body.p: No night spotlighting inside the reserve. No drones without a clearance that is almost never granted to tourists. No swimming within the buffer of a fishing camp. No feeding, calling or approaching wildlife. No plastic bottles in the boat - crews carry refill flasks, and you should refuse any single-use bottle handed to you on board. If an operator promises a tiger, leave: nobody can, and the promise tells you how they handle everything else.

Katka is the fastest, cheapest and most crowded; Haringata is the deer and mangrove-walk classic; Dublar Char gives you the big sandbank and the gharial banking area but depends on a good crossing; the Mongla side is quieter and better for birding, worse for the sunset shot everyone wants. For a first visit we run Katka-Haringata-Dublar over three nights. For a second visit, or for anyone who photographs, we go Mongla-side and stay two nights in one place rather than three in two.

October to March is the working window. April is hot and clear, good for early mornings. May onwards is cyclone-precaution season: boats may be held in port, the forest office may close a route mid-week, and we roll deposits forward rather than argue with the weather. The mangroves in June are greener and emptier than any postcard - if you can accept a boat that stops when the office says stop, the off-season is a real option.

author: Farhana Noor
title: Bangladesh month by month: a working table for planners
excerpt: Not a brochure version of the seasons - what closes, what opens, what is crowded, what the price does, and the two weeks in December you should avoid if you dislike crowds.

body.p: The country runs on three weather blocks and two festival spikes. Everything below assumes you are willing to move; if you need certainty, December to February on the coast and February to April in the north are the safest months.

The coast dries out, launch schedules to St. Martin’s open (usually a published first-Saturday after the cyclone window closes), hill trails firm up, and the haors start shrinking enough to reach the island villages by row-boat. Prices are at their base rate. This is our favourite two months for a first trip.

Dry, cool in the north (5-8 C at dawn in Rangpur and Sylhet; people are surprised), warm on the coast. The two weeks around 25 December to 5 January, and the Eid weekends, push Cox’s Bazar and Kuakata to peak rates and full hotels - if you want a beach in that window, book six to eight weeks out or go to the Kalapara side. Sundarban permits are the constraint here, not hotels.

Mango season in Rajshahi, hilsa at the river ghats, haze builds, and the tea country photographs beautifully in the morning before the heat flattens everything. St. Martin’s has to be booked back in February because the last launch of the season closes the island.

Monsoon. Waterfalls and haors at full volume, the Sundarbans green and empty, and beach swimming banned on many coasts. Ferries on the Padma may suspend on high flood, and hill tracks turn to soup. Hotels discount 30-40%. If you come in this season, plan around water, not against it.

Pohela Boishakh (mid-April) fills old Dhaka and Ramna. Durga Puja in October empties Khulna for two days and is the best urban photography of the year. Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha in the Gregorian drift are the two weekends when long-distance transport is genuinely difficult - book buses a week ahead, and do not schedule a travel day on the last day of Ramadan.

author: Priya Aich
title: Cox’s Bazar in the off-season: what you get and what you lose
excerpt: Half-price sea-view rooms, zero crowds, and a sea you must not swim in. A frank account of a July trip, with the safety rules the beach hotels should be giving you anyway.

body.p: In July the beach is 120 km of wet concrete-grey sand, the hotels have staff ratios that make December impossible, and the rip current is real and lethal. What you get is the actual town: fishermen mending nets where the jet skis normally run, and an Inani reef flat at low tide with nobody standing on it.

Where a red flag or a hotel lifeguard says no, the answer is no - the troughs off Laboni and Kolatoli shift after every squall. Rip current escape is the same everywhere: swim parallel, not against. Children on the sand are fine; children at the water edge are not our idea of a holiday.

Himchari’s waterfall is at its best and the temple steps are dry enough to walk. The Sugandha-to-Laboni sand walk is a good evening. Teknaf’s twin ridges will be clouded and worth trying anyway at first light. Inani is a tide-table trip: check the low water, walk the reef flat with shoes on, do not break or remove coral fragments, and leave before the tide turns - people get cut every year doing this in flip-flops.

Hotels discount 40-55%, boat operators discount far less because they have fewer trips to make, and food is unchanged. If a hotel offers you a package with "free" boat trip, ask what the trip actually costs in high season; the number is usually smaller than the discount.

author: Priya Aich
title: The five coral rules that keep St. Martin’s worth visiting
excerpt: Chhera’s reef flat is exposed for about ninety minutes a day. How to use that window without stepping on four hundred years of growth.

body.p: St. Martin’s is the only live coral reef system in Bangladesh, and the island is 8 km long with more beds than residents in season. The reef is not fragile in the way a painting is fragile; it is slow. A broken branch head that survives re-attaches in years, and a trampled flat takes decades.

One: no fins or hard-soled shoes in the water on the flat - booties or bare feet. Two: never stand on coral; find sand, or float. Three: nothing leaves the water, alive, dead or bleached, including "pretty" branches on the beach. Four: no sunscreen within thirty minutes of entering if you can avoid it - the reef flat is shallow and the chemicals are not neutral; a shirt is better than cream. Five: no boats closer than the marked line at the south end while turtle nesting is monitored.

Chhera landing is allowed at published low tide only. We schedule the ninety-minute window and tell you when it closes; if a boatman offers to "just take you to the far side", decline. The far side is where the nursery colonies are.

Snorkel the sand-rimmed edges with a mask that fits, take the south-end cycle loop, and go to the island’s small Hindu temple at Uttar para in the evening, which is the best reason to be on Martin’s at all: it is the reason the island has had a settled community for centuries instead of being only a resort.

author: Mashzidul Tanun Borshon
title: Inside the haors: travelling Bangladesh’s seasonal inland seas
excerpt: Tangaur holds 100 times the water of Sylhet’s floods in March. What it means for roads, boats, birds, and for anyone who expects a normal itinerary.

body.p: A haor is a bowl that becomes a sea. In the wet months the Sylhet-Sunamganj plain holds a body of water you can lose the far shore in, and the villages sit on raised platforms with boats tied to the veranda. In winter it is green farmland with a thread of river in the middle. Both versions are worth a trip; only one of them fits a fixed schedule.

Between June and September, roads to the haor belt are passable but slow: allow the Sunamganj run as five hours from Sylhet rather than three. Small boats replace vehicles on the last leg to Tangaur and Bazaratung, and rain can strand you for a night - which is why we build a buffer day and hotel relationships in Sunamganj rather than promising a same-day return.

The wet season list is the reason to come: greater adjutant storks nest on the tall trees of the village islands (locals call them "hargila"), and the open water brings large flocks of waders and ducks. Bring binoculars; a 400 mm lens is happy; the boatman will know the trees where the birds roost.

Flat light over flat water is dull, so shoot at first and last light and use the embankment roads as leading lines. The best single image of the haor country is a morning silhouette of a rowing family against a flooded field. Ask before photographing faces; we pay a small model fee when someone poses, and we think every photographer should.

Do not touch or feed the storks. Do not ask a boatman to run a nesting bird down. Buy food and tea in the village rather than eating packed rations, and if you hire a boat, hire the family’s boat rather than haggling a stranger down to Tk 200. The margin is what keeps the boats on the water.

author: Shahanur Rahman
title: The north Bengal heritage triangle in one very long day
excerpt: Paharpur at opening, Mahasthangarh at noon, Kantajiu at golden hour: 260 km, three UNESCO-grade sites and one temple front, with the light windows that make it work.

body.p: It can be done from Rajshahi in a single day if you start at 05:30 and accept that you are trading depth for distance. Two nights and three sites is better; this is the emergency version, written because guests keep asking for it.

Somapura Mahavihara is the largest Buddhist monastery south of the Himalayas and the plan is the reason it is on the World Heritage list: a cruciform court of 177 cells around a central temple-mound. At opening the light is low and rakes across the burnt-brick courses, which is the only way to see the construction lines. The site museum holds the terracotta originals, including the dancing figures and the graffito pots - do not skip it for time; fifteen minutes is enough.

The fortified city is a continuous occupation from the 3rd century BCE, and the visible circuit is 1.5 km of rampart with a moat outside. Start at the Deva Angana platform, walk the western bastion, then the Balial Dighi tank, and finish at the site museum for the Mahendraparvata inscription and the Gupta-period terracottas. The Pakhi Keshura mosque and the Mazar are inside the circuit - both are living sites; dress and behave accordingly, and do not photograph the prayer hall.

A single-family Krishna temple at Dinajpur, built 1704-1722, and the densest surviving example of narrative terracotta in Bengal: the south face alone carries Ramayana and Krishna episodes stacked in registers, with contemporary figures in the lowest band - palanquins, boats, a ship under sail. At 16:30 in winter the sun lights the south face directly, and the modelling reads at two metres for the first time in the day. Photograph without flash; the terracotta is fired clay but the surface crust is not indestructible.

You will read about Puthia, Bagha and Choto Sona at speed or not at all, and the drive from Dinajpur back to Rajshahi takes three hours after dark on good roads. We would rather you gave it two days; if you cannot, we still arrange it, and we will give you a driver who has done the run before at that hour.
